section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: Which of the following best facilitated British colonization of North America?
options: (A) The Columbian exchange
(B) The defeat of the Spanish Armada
(C) The encomienda system
(D) The period of salutary neglect
items.explanation: England's defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 broke Spain's naval dominance and opened the Atlantic to English colonization. Before that victory, Spain's sea power had kept rivals from challenging its New World monopoly; afterward, England could safely send colonists to North America. The Armada's destruction cleared the ocean path that made Jamestown and the later colonies possible.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Columbian exchange was the transfer of plants, animals, and diseases — it did not facilitate England's colonizing ability.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Defeating the Spanish Armada in 1588 removed the naval obstacle to English colonization of North America.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The encomienda was Spain's forced-labor system, not an aid to British colonization.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Salutary neglect came much later and described Britain's loose administration, not what first enabled colonization.

items.stem: Bradford's account of Squanto illustrates The 1914 painting above depicts the harvest feast symbolizing Native aid to the Pilgrims described in Bradford's account.

stimulus.image_caption: Jennie Augusta Brownscombe, 'The First Thanksgiving at Plymouth,' 1914.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Jennie Augusta Brownscombe, 1914; pre-1930 publication
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following excerpt.

"Squanto... was a special instrument sent of God for their good beyond their expectation. He directed them how to set their corn, where to take fish, and to procure other commodities, and was also their pilot to bring them to unknown places for their profit, and never left them till he died."
—William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation (abridged)

options: A. The complete absence of Native-colonist contact
B. The total military dominance of the Pilgrims
C. The critical role of Native aid in colonial survival
D. Spanish missionary influence in New England
items.explanation: William Bradford's account credits Squanto — the Patuxet Indian who had learned English — with teaching the Pilgrims to plant corn, fish, and survive the New England wilderness. Without that Native aid, the struggling Plymouth colony would likely have starved as earlier settlements had. Bradford's story is fundamentally about dependence: the Pilgrims survived because Native people helped them.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Bradford describes extensive contact and aid, not an absence of it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Pilgrims were militarily weak newcomers; Bradford's account shows dependence, not dominance.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Bradford's account of Squanto illustrates the critical role of Native aid in colonial survival.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Spanish missionaries had no presence in New England; this was an English-Patuxet encounter.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how Cortes's few hundred men were able to carry out the actions described in the passage?

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"In these chapels are the images or idols... the principal ones, in which the people have greatest faith and confidence, I precipitated from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, as they were all polluted with human blood, shed in the sacrifices. In the places of these I put images of our Lady and the Saints... I answered, through the interpreters, that they were deceived in expecting any favors from idols, the work of their own hands... and that they must learn there was but one God, the universal Lord of all, who had created the heavens and earth, and all things else, and had made them and us."
—Hernando Cortés, Second Letter to Charles V, October 30, 1520 (abridged)

options: A. A Spanish field army that greatly outnumbered the Aztec forces
B. The Aztec Empire's lack of any organized system of warfare
C. Indigenous alliances against Aztec rule, combined with steel weapons, horses, and firearms
D. The conversion of the Aztec priesthood to Christianity before 1520
items.explanation: Cortés commanded only a few hundred Spaniards against an empire of millions — his victory is explained by allies, not numbers. Subject peoples who hated Aztec domination, especially the Tlaxcalans, supplied tens of thousands of warriors, while Spanish steel swords, horses, and firearms gave the small force a terrifying edge. The conquest was a Native alliance armed with European technology, not a Spanish army overwhelming the Aztecs alone.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. No Spanish field army outnumbered the Aztecs; Cortés's force was tiny and depended on Native allies.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Aztecs had a sophisticated military system; their defeat was not due to lacking organized warfare.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Indigenous alliances against Aztec rule, combined with steel weapons, horses, and firearms, explain the Spanish success.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Aztec priesthood was not converted before 1520; Cortés was still smashing their idols, as the passage shows.

items.stem: The creation of the Dominion of New England The 1684 portrait above shows James II, the king who created the Dominion of New England.

stimulus.image_caption: James II of England, by Sir Godfrey Kneller, 1684.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Sir Godfrey Kneller, 1684; pre-1930

options: A. Increased democracy in the colonies
B. Strengthened the governor's authority in the region
C. Let New England colonies air common grievances
D. Placed the king in direct control of New England affairs
items.explanation: James II created the Dominion of New England in 1686 by revoking colonial charters and merging the colonies under a single royal governor, Edmund Andros. The move abolished elected assemblies and town meetings — it put the king in direct control of New England affairs. Colonists experienced it as tyranny, and they overthrew it in 1689 when news of the Glorious Revolution arrived.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Dominion abolished elected assemblies; it reduced democracy, not increased it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Dominion replaced local governors with one royal appointee; it did not strengthen existing governors' authority.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Dominion silenced colonial grievances by eliminating assemblies, not by giving them a forum.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Dominion of New England placed the king in direct control of New England affairs.

items.stem: Whitefield’s revival meetings contributed most directly to which of the following trends?

stimulus.text: “As for the lawfulness of keeping slaves, I have no doubt, since I hear of some that were bought with Abraham’s money, and some that were born in his house.—And I cannot help thinking, that some of those servants mentioned by the Apostles in their epistles, were or had been slaves. It is plain, that the Gibeonites were doomed to perpetual slavery, and though liberty is a sweet thing to such as are born free, yet to those who never knew the sweets of it, slavery perhaps may not be so irksome.” Source: George Whitefield, 1751

options: (A) Republican Motherhood
(B) Political and religious independence
(C) Back-to-the-land migration
(D) Progressive social reforms
items.explanation: George Whitefield's Great Awakening revivals taught ordinary colonists to trust their own spiritual judgment over established authority — to question ministers, reject old hierarchies, and decide for themselves. That habit of challenging authority carried into politics: colonists who had defied religious establishments found it easier to defy Parliament. The revivals' deepest contribution was training Americans in political and religious independence.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Republican Motherhood was a post-Revolution idea about women's civic role, not a product of Whitefield's revivals.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Whitefield's revivals encouraged colonists to question established authority, fostering political and religious independence.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Back-to-the-land migration was not the trend Whitefield's urban and frontier revivals produced.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Progressive reforms came a century and a half later, in the early 1900s.

items.stem: The column erected by the French commander in the image most directly signified which of the following?

stimulus.image_caption: Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Theodor de Bry after Jacques Le Moyne, 1591; Library of Congress, pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 5-8 refer to the image above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: (A) {'letter': 'A', 'text': 'European plans to convert the Native Americans to Christianity'}
(B) {'letter': 'B', 'text': 'European hopes for trade in new products'}
(C) {'letter': 'C', 'text': 'European claims to political control over new territory'}
(D) {'letter': 'D', 'text': 'European interest in sharing Native American culture'}
items.explanation: When French explorers like Cartier planted a column or cross on foreign shores, they were performing a legal ritual: taking possession of the territory for the French king. The column was not about trade, conversion, or cultural exchange — it was a marker of sovereignty, announcing to rival Europeans that this land was now claimed. Such ceremonies were how early modern empires asserted political control over new territory.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The column was a claim of possession, not a missionary project to convert Native peoples.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Trade hopes were real, but the column itself signified a political claim, not commercial plans.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The column signified European claims to political control over new territory.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The ceremony asserted French sovereignty; it was not an expression of interest in sharing Native culture.

items.stem: All of the following are examples of conflicts between colonists and Native American tribes EXCEPT
options: (A) Bacon’s Rebellion
(B) the Pequot War
(C) the Stono Uprising
(D) King Philip’s War
items.explanation: Bacon's Rebellion (1676), the Pequot War (1637), and King Philip's War (1675–1676) were all violent conflicts between English colonists and Native peoples. The Stono Uprising (1739) was different: it was a rebellion of enslaved Africans in South Carolina against their enslavers. It belongs to the history of slavery and resistance, not to the history of colonist-Native warfare.

option_explanations.A: This was a colonist-Native conflict, so it is not the answer. Bacon's Rebellion involved fighting against Native peoples.
option_explanations.B: This was a colonist-Native conflict, so it is not the answer. The Pequot War was English colonists against the Pequot tribe.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The Stono Uprising was an enslaved-African rebellion against slaveholders, not a colonist-Native conflict.
option_explanations.D: This was a colonist-Native conflict, so it is not the answer. King Philip's War was the bloodiest colonist-Native war in New England.

items.stem: The law referenced above was meant to accomplish all of the following EXCEPT

stimulus.text: “And it hath accordingly happened that an open resistance to the execution of the laws hath actually taken place in the town of Boston, and the neighbourhood thereof, within the said province: And whereas it is, under these circumstances, become absolutely necessary…that the said method of annually electing the counsellors or assistants of the said province should no longer be suffered to continue but that the appointment of the said counsellors or assistants should henceforth be put upon the like footing as is established in such other of his Majesty’s colonies or plantations in America, the governors whereof are appointed by his Majesty’s commission, under the great seal of Great Britain…so much of the charter, granted by their majesties King William and Queen Mary to the inhabitants of the said province of the Massachusetts Bay, in New England, and all and every clause…be revoked…and that the offices of all counsellors and assistants, elected and appointed in pursuance thereof, shall from thenceforth cease and determine: And that, the council, or court of assistants of the said province for the time being, shall be composed of such of the inhabitants or proprietors of lands within the same as shall be thereunto nominated and appointed by his Majesty…” Source: The Coercive Acts, 1774

options: (A) provide Britain with the ability to select governing officials in the Massachusetts Bay Colony
(B) require the quartering of Britain’s officials and military in the homes of Massachusetts Bay residents
(C) revoke the rule of governance outlined in the Massachusetts Bay Charter
(D) punish the Massachusetts Bay Colony for the events of the Boston Tea Party
items.explanation: The quoted law is the Massachusetts Government Act, one of the Coercive Acts: it let Britain appoint Massachusetts officials, revoked the charter's elected council, and aimed to punish Boston for the Tea Party. Quartering troops in private homes was the business of a different measure — the Quartering Act. The excerpt's law did not require household quartering; that was a separate act's provision.

option_explanations.A: The law was meant to do this, so it is not the answer. It gave Britain power to select Massachusetts officials.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Quartering in private homes belonged to the separate Quartering Act, not to the law quoted here.
option_explanations.C: The law was meant to do this, so it is not the answer. It revoked the Massachusetts Bay Charter's governance rules.
option_explanations.D: The law was meant to do this, so it is not the answer. Punishing Boston for the Tea Party was its explicit purpose.

items.stem: The meeting pictured in the painting above included articulations of all of the following EXCEPT

stimulus.pd_rationale: John Trumbull, 1819; pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The painting above (replacing the bare title reference): Trumbull's 'Declaration of Independence' (1818-1819).

options: (A) the laws of governance to be used in the newly formed United States
(B) principles of individual liberties and rights of people
(C) grievances against the British Crown
(D) justification for why the American colonies should independently self-govern
items.explanation: The painting depicts the First Continental Congress of 1774, which articulated colonial rights, listed grievances against the Crown, and justified resistance — but stopped short of independence. What it did not do was write the laws of governance for a new United States; in 1774 the delegates still sought redress within the empire, not a new nation's constitution. Founding a new government's laws came later, with independence.

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The 1774 meeting did not establish laws of governance for a newly formed United States.
option_explanations.B: The meeting did articulate these, so it is not the answer. Rights and liberties were central to its declarations.
option_explanations.C: The meeting did articulate these, so it is not the answer. Grievances against the Crown filled its petitions.
option_explanations.D: The meeting did articulate this, so it is not the answer. It justified colonial self-government, though not yet full independence.

items.stem: Franklin's argument rests on the assumption that

stimulus.text:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"I am for doing good to the poor, but ... I think the best way of doing good to the poor, is not making them easy in poverty, but leading or driving them out of it."
—Benjamin Franklin, 1766 (abridged)

options: A. Idleness, not circumstance, is the main cause of poverty
B. Colonial governments should expand poor relief
C. Wealth is inherently immoral
D. The British crown should fund colonial workhouses
items.explanation: Franklin argues that the best poor relief is not making poverty comfortable but driving people out of it — an argument that assumes poverty comes mainly from idleness rather than from circumstances beyond the poor's control. If misfortune caused poverty, easing it would be kindness; Franklin instead treats comfort as the problem and industry as the cure. His whole position rests on blaming idleness, not circumstance.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Franklin assumes idleness, not circumstance, is the main cause of poverty.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Franklin opposes expanding poor relief; he wants to make poverty uncomfortable to spur industry.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Franklin does not condemn wealth; he celebrates industry and its rewards.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Franklin is not asking the Crown to fund workhouses; his argument is about the philosophy of relief.

items.stem: The painting above highlights which of the following developments from 1800 to 1848?

stimulus.pd_rationale: John Trumbull, 1819; pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The painting above: Trumbull's 'Declaration of Independence' (1818-1819).

options: (A) The development of a national and distinctive American culture
(B) The growth of political and sectional divisions
(C) The notion that humanity can be perfected through reform movements
(D) The growing conviction that slavery is a sin
items.explanation: The painting highlights the emergence between 1800 and 1848 of a national and distinctive American culture — in literature, art, and thought. This was the era of the Hudson River School painters, of Emerson and the Transcendentalists, of a self-consciously American voice distinct from Europe's. The cultural nationalism of the period expressed a young republic defining itself artistically.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The painting highlights the development of a national and distinctive American culture in this period.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Sectional divisions were growing, but the painting celebrates cultural achievement, not political fracture.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Reform movements were active, but the painting's subject is cultural distinctiveness, not human perfectibility.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Antislavery conviction was growing, but the painting highlights cultural nationalism, not abolitionism.

items.stem: Logan's speech best illustrates which of the following?

stimulus.text:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following excerpt.

"I appeal to any white man to say if ever he entered Logan's cabin hungry and he gave him not meat... During the course of the last long and bloody war Logan remained idle in his cabin, an advocate for peace... I had even thought to have lived with you but for the injuries of one man. Colonel Cresap, the last spring, in cold blood and unprovoked, murdered all the relations of Logan... There runs not a drop of my blood in the veins of any living creature. This called on me for revenge. I have sought it. I have killed many... But do not harbor a thought that mine is the joy of fear. Logan never felt fear."
—Logan (Tah-gah-jute), speech recorded 1774 (abridged)

options: A. Native leaders uniformly rejected all diplomacy and negotiation with colonists
B. British officials successfully mediated frontier disputes between settlers and tribes
C. Cycles of personal revenge and retaliatory violence shaped frontier relations
D. The Proclamation of 1763 permanently ended all frontier violence
items.explanation: Logan's speech is the story of a personal cycle: Cresap's men murdered his family, and Logan answered with revenge killings of his own. Peace advocacy gave way to retaliation, which would invite further retaliation. The speech captures how frontier relations worked in practice — not through treaties or mediation, but through spirals of personal revenge and retaliatory violence.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Logan himself had been an advocate for peace; his speech shows diplomacy abandoned, not uniformly rejected.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. No British mediation resolved this; Logan's story is one of unmediated revenge.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Logan's speech illustrates cycles of personal revenge and retaliatory violence on the frontier.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Proclamation of 1763 did not end frontier violence, as Logan's 1774 experience proves.

items.stem: Which of the following most accurately describes the general colonial public’s response to the attitudes described in the excerpt above?

stimulus.image_caption: Benjamin Franklin, 'Join, or Die,' Pennsylvania Gazette, May 9, 1754.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Benjamin Franklin, 1754; pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The image above: Franklin's 'Join, or Die' cartoon of May 9, 1754.

options: (A) Most colonists considered the war against Great Britain necessary and openly supported its efforts.
(B) Most colonists viewed the Declaration of Independence with apprehension and were sympathetic to British interests in the colonies.
(C) Most colonists were largely indifferent and wished for resolution of the rising hostilities as fast as possible.
(D) Most colonists were enslaved people and resisted for calls of independence viewing the British as more likely to grant them liberty.
items.explanation: Historians estimate that only about a third of colonists actively supported independence, a third remained loyal to Britain, and a third tried to stay out of it. Most ordinary colonists were not ideologues but people hoping the troubles would end quickly so they could get on with their lives. Indifference and a wish for speedy resolution — not passionate commitment — described the colonial majority.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Only a minority openly supported the war effort; most colonists were not committed patriots.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Most colonists were not anxiously pro-British; they were uncommitted and war-weary.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Most colonists were largely indifferent and wished for a fast resolution of the hostilities.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Most colonists were not enslaved people; the indifferent majority was free.

items.stem: George Washington established the principle of executive privilege in a dispute with Congress over the
options: (A) Alien and Sedition Acts
(B) legality of political parties
(C) Jay Treaty
(D) Whiskey Rebellion
items.explanation: When Congress demanded papers relating to the Jay Treaty in 1796, Washington refused — asserting that the president could withhold executive communications from Congress. That refusal established the principle of executive privilege: the president's right to keep certain deliberations confidential. The Jay Treaty fight, not the Alien and Sedition Acts or the Whiskey Rebellion, was the occasion.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Alien and Sedition Acts came under John Adams, after Washington left office.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The legality of parties was debated, but executive privilege arose over treaty documents.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Washington established executive privilege in the dispute with Congress over the Jay Treaty.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Whiskey Rebellion tested federal military power, not presidential confidentiality.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would have been most supportive of the excerpt above?

stimulus.text: “And it hath accordingly happened that an open resistance to the execution of the laws hath actually taken place in the town of Boston, and the neighbourhood thereof, within the said province: And whereas it is, under these circumstances, become absolutely necessary…that the said method of annually electing the counsellors or assistants of the said province should no longer be suffered to continue but that the appointment of the said counsellors or assistants should henceforth be put upon the like footing as is established in such other of his Majesty’s colonies or plantations in America, the governors whereof are appointed by his Majesty’s commission, under the great seal of Great Britain…so much of the charter, granted by their majesties King William and Queen Mary to the inhabitants of the said province of the Massachusetts Bay, in New England, and all and every clause…be revoked…and that the offices of all counsellors and assistants, elected and appointed in pursuance thereof, shall from thenceforth cease and determine: And that, the council, or court of assistants of the said province for the time being, shall be composed of such of the inhabitants or proprietors of lands within the same as shall be thereunto nominated and appointed by his Majesty…” Source: The Coercive Acts, 1774

options: (A) A participant in the Boston Tea Party
(B) A delegate to the Stamp Act Congress
(C) A colonial tax collector
(D) An elected member of a colonial legislature
items.explanation: The Coercive Acts crushed Massachusetts's self-government to punish Boston for the Tea Party — a policy its supporters cheered. A colonial tax collector, dependent on British authority and hated by the patriots, would welcome laws that strengthened the Crown's hand and disciplined the rebellious colony. The excerpt's punitive spirit matched the loyalist official's interests exactly.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. A Boston Tea Party participant was the target of these punitive acts, not their supporter.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. A Stamp Act Congress delegate had protested British taxation a decade earlier.
option_explanations.C: Correct. A colonial tax collector — a Crown official — would most support the Coercive Acts' punishment of Massachusetts.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. An elected legislator would see the acts as an attack on representative government itself.

items.stem: As a result of Jefferson's election in 1800,
options: A. Increased aid to the commercial sector
B. Made foreign policy more pro-British
C. Drove the federal debt sharply upward
D. Eliminated federal excise taxes
items.explanation: Jefferson's election in 1800 brought the Democratic-Republicans to power on a platform of small government and low taxes. Their signature domestic achievement was eliminating the Federalists' excise taxes — including the hated whiskey tax — shrinking federal revenue and the government's reach. The Revolution of 1800 meant fewer taxes, not more aid, debt, or British alignment.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Jefferson cut government support for commerce; aiding the commercial sector was Hamilton's program.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Jefferson's foreign policy tilted toward France, not Britain.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Jefferson reduced the federal debt; he did not drive it sharply upward.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Jefferson's election led to the elimination of federal excise taxes.

items.stem: In the decade after this image was published, the Cherokee experienced which of the following?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1838 (I. T. Bowen, Philadelphia; McKenney-Hall series). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed on Commons file page (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) The Cherokee were forcibly relocated to Indian Territory in the West.
(B) The Cherokee secured permanent, long-lasting reservations inside Georgia.
(C) Disease and warfare eliminated the Cherokee as a people.
(D) The federal government revoked the Cherokee's status as a recognized tribe.
items.explanation: In the decade after the image's publication, the Cherokee suffered forced removal: the Indian Removal Act, Georgia's land grab, and the Supreme Court's unenforced Worcester decision culminated in the Trail of Tears of 1838–1839, when federal troops drove the Cherokee to Indian Territory. Thousands died on the march. The image's hopeful depiction of Cherokee adaptation gave way to expulsion.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Cherokee were forcibly relocated to Indian Territory in the West — the Trail of Tears.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Georgia did not grant permanent reservations; it seized Cherokee land.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Cherokee survived as a people, though removal was catastrophic.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Cherokee's tribal status was not revoked; they were removed westward as a nation.

items.stem: Jefferson's Louisiana Purchase contradicted his strict constructionism because

stimulus.text:
Questions 49–52 refer to the following quotation.

"The man who mounted the steps of the Capitol, March 4, 1801 … Jefferson was very tall, six feet two-and-a-half inches in height; sandy-complexioned; shy in manner, seeming cold; awkward in attitude … this loose, shackling person … belonged to the controlling influences of American history." —Henry Adams, History of the United States During the Administration of Thomas Jefferson, 1889 (abridged)

options: A. France refused to sell Louisiana
B. Congress unanimously opposed the purchase
C. It expanded slavery into New England
D. The Constitution nowhere authorized purchasing foreign territory
items.explanation: Jefferson was a strict constructionist who believed the federal government could do only what the Constitution explicitly authorized — and the Constitution says nothing about buying foreign territory. Yet he seized the Louisiana opportunity anyway, admitting privately that he was stretching his principles. The purchase contradicted his constitutional theory precisely because no clause authorized it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. France was eager to sell; Napoleon's offer is what made the purchase possible.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Congress approved the purchase; opposition was not unanimous.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The purchase did not expand slavery into New England; it opened western territories.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The purchase contradicted strict constructionism because the Constitution nowhere authorized buying foreign territory.

items.stem: By what means did the United States take possession of the Oregon Territory?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1846 by John Haven. Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) The United States was granted the territory in a postwar treaty with France.
(B) The United States bought it from the Native Americans who lived there.
(C) U.S. settlers were the first to arrive in the region; they claimed it for their country.
(D) Great Britain ceded it to the United States as part of a negotiated treaty.
items.explanation: The Oregon Territory was claimed by both Britain and the United States until the Oregon Treaty of 1846 divided it at the 49th parallel. Britain ceded its claim to the southern portion — the future Oregon, Washington, and Idaho — through negotiation, not war or purchase. Diplomacy, with the slogan Fifty-four Forty or Fight as backdrop, settled the boundary.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. France had no claim on Oregon; the territory was disputed with Britain.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The United States did not buy Oregon from Native peoples; it negotiated with Britain.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. American settlers arrived, but possession came through the treaty with Britain, not mere arrival.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Great Britain ceded its claim to the Oregon Territory through the negotiated treaty of 1846.

items.stem: The Know-Nothing Party focused its efforts almost exclusively on the issue of
options: (A) the right to bear arms
(B) the prohibition of alcohol
(C) women’s rights
(D) immigration
items.explanation: The Know-Nothing Party — the American Party — was a single-issue movement: it existed to oppose immigration, especially Irish and German Catholic newcomers. Its platform demanded longer naturalization waits, immigration restrictions, and barring Catholics from office. Every other issue was secondary to the nativist crusade against foreigners.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Gun rights were not the Know-Nothings' issue; immigration was.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Prohibition was a temperance cause, not the Know-Nothing focus.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Women's rights were not the Know-Nothings' concern.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Know-Nothing Party focused almost exclusively on immigration.

items.stem: Seguin's role as a Tejano officer honoring the Alamo dead most directly complicates which simplistic narrative?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Painted 1844 by Theodore Gentilz. Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following quotation.

"Companions in arms! These remains which we have the honor of carrying on our shoulders are those of the valiant heroes who died in the Alamo. Yes, my friends, they preferred death to bondage..."
—Colonel Juan N. Seguin, oration, 1837 (abridged)

options: A. That the Alamo's defenders all survived
B. That Texas joined the Union immediately
C. That the Texas Revolution was purely Anglo versus Mexican
D. That Mexico supported Texan independence
items.explanation: Juan Seguín was a Tejano — a Mexican Texan — who fought for Texas independence and later honored the Alamo dead as an officer. His presence breaks the simple story of Anglos versus Mexicans: the Texas Revolution included Tejanos fighting alongside Anglo settlers against Santa Anna's central government. The conflict was political, not purely ethnic, and Seguín proves it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Alamo's defenders famously died; Seguín's role does not suggest they survived.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Texas waited nine years for annexation; Seguín's story is not about the timing of statehood.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Seguín complicates the narrative that the Texas Revolution was purely Anglo versus Mexican.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Mexico opposed Texan independence; Santa Anna's army besieged the Alamo.

items.stem: The Marbury v. Madison decision
options: A. Expanded presidential powers claimed by Jefferson's Republicans
B. Gave broad new powers to state courts
C. Upheld the Alien and Sedition Acts
D. Established the principle of judicial review
items.explanation: Marbury v. Madison (1803) arose from a dispute over undelivered judicial appointments, but Chief Justice John Marshall used it to establish something far larger: the Supreme Court's power to strike down acts of Congress that violate the Constitution. That principle — judicial review — made the Court the final arbiter of constitutionality and a co-equal branch of government.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Marbury limited, not expanded, Jefferson's Republicans by asserting judicial power over them.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The decision empowered the federal Supreme Court, not state courts.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Alien and Sedition Acts were not at issue in Marbury.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Marbury v. Madison established the principle of judicial review.

items.stem: Fillmore's letter combined with Perry's 'powerful squadron' best illustrates which of the following?

stimulus.text: "The United States of America reach from ocean to ocean, and our Territory of Oregon and State of California lie directly opposite to the dominions of your imperial majesty. Our steamships can go from California to Japan in eighteen days.... I am desirous that our two countries should trade with each other, for the benefit both of Japan and the United States.... These are the only objects for which I have sent Commodore Perry, with a powerful squadron, to pay a visit to your imperial majesty's renowned city of Yedo: friendship, commerce, a supply of coal and provisions, and protection for our shipwrecked people." — President Millard Fillmore, letter to the Emperor of Japan, delivered by Commodore Matthew Perry, 1853

options: (A) American diplomacy backed by the implicit threat of force — gunboat diplomacy.
(B) Japan's eager initiative in seeking American trade goods.
(C) A purely peaceful program of cultural exchange with Japan.
(D) Congressional opposition to any American expansion in the Pacific.
items.explanation: Fillmore's letter speaks of friendship and commerce, but it was delivered by Perry's powerful squadron — warships anchored off the Japanese coast. The message was unmistakable: open your ports to American trade, or face the guns. That combination of diplomatic courtesy and naval menace is gunboat diplomacy: negotiation backed by the implicit threat of force.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Fillmore's letter plus Perry's squadron illustrates gunboat diplomacy — diplomacy backed by the implicit threat of force.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Japan did not seek American trade; the shogunate resisted opening until confronted.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The powerful squadron made this anything but purely peaceful cultural exchange.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Congress did not oppose Pacific expansion; the expedition was official American policy.

items.stem: “Bleeding Kansas” was a direct result of the doctrine of

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published c.1856 (Wm. C. Reynolds, New York). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) judicial review
(B) imperialism
(C) containment
(D) popular sovereignty
items.explanation: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) let settlers decide slavery's fate by popular sovereignty — and the result was Bleeding Kansas, as proslavery and antislavery settlers rushed in and turned the territory into a battleground. Letting the issue be voted on did not settle it; it armed it. The violence was the direct fruit of the popular-sovereignty doctrine.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Judicial review was not the doctrine behind Bleeding Kansas.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Imperialism was not the cause of Kansas's sectional violence.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Containment was a Cold War doctrine, a century later.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Bleeding Kansas resulted directly from the doctrine of popular sovereignty.

items.stem: Lincoln's distinction between containing slavery and abolishing it reflected

stimulus.text:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following quotation.

"Wrong as we think slavery is, we can yet afford to leave it alone where it is … but can we, while our votes will prevent it, allow it to spread into the National Territories, and to overrun us here in these Free States? … LET US HAVE FAITH THAT RIGHT MAKES MIGHT, AND IN THAT FAITH, LET US, TO THE END, DARE TO DO OUR DUTY AS WE UNDERSTAND IT." —Abraham Lincoln, Cooper Union Address, February 27, 1860 (abridged)

options: A. Support for slavery's expansion
B. Indifference to the slavery question
C. A plan for immediate emancipation
D. A strategy to unite antislavery voters without alarming moderates
items.explanation: Lincoln's Cooper Union position — slavery is wrong, but the federal government should only stop its spread, not abolish it where it existed — was crafted to hold a coalition. It united committed antislavery voters behind containment while reassuring moderates and border-state men that Lincoln was no radical abolitionist. The distinction was political strategy: maximum antislavery unity, minimum alarm.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Lincoln opposed slavery's expansion; he did not support it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Lincoln cared intensely about slavery; his position was strategic, not indifferent.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Lincoln explicitly disavowed immediate emancipation in 1860.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The distinction was a strategy to unite antislavery voters without alarming moderates.

items.stem: The Fifteenth Amendment

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1870 (lithograph after James C. Beard; Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; PD tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: A. Readmitted Southern states to the Union
B. Abolished slavery
C. Barred racial discrimination in voting
D. Disqualified ex-Confederate officials from office
items.explanation: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) provides that the right to vote shall not be denied on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. It was the Reconstruction amendment that attacked racial discrimination at the ballot box — the legal foundation for Black suffrage. It did not end slavery (Thirteenth), define citizenship (Fourteenth), or readmit states; its subject was voting.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Readmitting Southern states was accomplished through Reconstruction Acts and state constitutions, not this amendment.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Slavery was abolished by the Thirteenth Amendment, not the Fifteenth.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Fifteenth Amendment barred racial discrimination in voting.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Disqualifying ex-Confederates was the Fourteenth Amendment's Section 3, not the Fifteenth.

items.stem: An important consequence of the Black Codes was which of the following?
options: (A) They convinced many Republicans that a more thorough federal Reconstruction was needed.
(B) They triggered an immediate mass migration of Black Southerners to Northern cities.
(C) They led the Supreme Court to become the chief defender of Black constitutional rights.
(D) They persuaded President Johnson to install Union generals as Southern governors.
items.explanation: The Black Codes — Southern laws restricting freedpeople's movement, labor, and rights — proved to Northern Republicans that the South intended to restore slavery in everything but name. Rather than accepting Johnson's lenient Reconstruction, Republicans concluded that only thorough federal intervention could secure freedom's substance. The Codes were the provocation that drove Congress to seize control of Reconstruction.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Black Codes convinced many Republicans that a more thorough federal Reconstruction was needed.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The great Black migration North came decades later, during World War I, not immediately after the Codes.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Supreme Court of this era generally undermined Black rights; it did not become their chief defender.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Johnson did not install Union generals as governors in response to the Codes; Congress imposed military Reconstruction over his veto.

items.stem: Stowe's method of awakening sympathy through stories of suffering was most similar to that of

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1852 (first-edition title page). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"The object of these sketches is to awaken sympathy and feeling for the African race, as they exist among us; to show their wrongs and sorrows, under a system so necessarily cruel and unjust as to defeat and do away the good effects of all that can be attempted for them."
—Harriet Beecher Stowe, preface to Uncle Tom's Cabin, 1852 (abridged)

options: A. Phrenology textbooks classifying human skulls
B. Railroad timetables coordinating travel
C. Minstrel shows caricaturing Black life for entertainment
D. Abolitionist slave narratives such as Frederick Douglass's Narrative
items.explanation: Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin awakened Northern sympathy by telling stories of enslaved people's suffering — the same method abolitionist slave narratives had pioneered. Frederick Douglass's Narrative and similar accounts used firsthand stories of cruelty to make slavery's evil vivid and personal. Stowe, a white novelist, borrowed the slave narrative's emotional machinery: suffering rendered in story to move readers' hearts.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Phrenology textbooks classified skulls pseudoscientifically; they did not awaken sympathy through stories.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Railroad timetables were practical documents, not instruments of moral persuasion.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Minstrel shows mocked Black life for white entertainment — the opposite of Stowe's sympathetic method.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Stowe's method most resembled abolitionist slave narratives like Douglass's, using stories of suffering to awaken sympathy.

items.stem: The Act's funding mechanism — federal land grants to build state colleges — reflected which constitutional vision?

stimulus.text:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following quotation.

"Be it enacted ... That there be granted to the several States, for the purposes hereinafter mentioned, an amount of public land, to be apportioned to each State a quantity equal to thirty thousand acres for each senator and representative..."
—Morrill Land-Grant Act, 1862 (abridged)

options: A. Strict states' rights
B. Diplomatic isolationism
C. Laissez-faire with no federal aid
D. An expansive federal role in economic development
items.explanation: The Morrill Act used federal land — a national resource — to fund colleges in every state, building the country's educational infrastructure from Washington. That is the Hamiltonian vision in action: an expansive federal role in economic development, with the national government actively shaping growth rather than leaving it to the states or the market alone. Land grants were federal power deployed for national purposes.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Strict states' rights would leave such projects to the states; federal land grants assert national power.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Diplomatic isolationism concerns foreign policy, not domestic college funding.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Federal land grants are the opposite of laissez-faire; they are active government aid.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The funding mechanism reflected an expansive federal role in economic development.

items.stem: In what way did the actions of Abraham Lincoln in 1860 contradict Douglass’s sentiments in the excerpt above?

stimulus.text: “In one view the slaveholders have a decided advantage over all opposition. It is well to notice this advantage—the advantage of complete organization. They are organized; and yet were not at the pains of creating their organizations. The State governments, where the system of slavery exists, are complete slavery organizations. The church organizations in those States are equally at the service of slavery; while the Federal Government, with its army and navy, from the chief magistracy in Washington, to the Supreme Court, and thence to the chief marshalship at New York, is pledged to support, defend, and propagate the crying curse of human bondage. The pen, the purse, and the sword, are united against the simple truth, preached by humble men in obscure places.” Source: Frederick Douglass, “The Dred Scott Decision” (speech), 1857 (public domain).

options: (A) Lincoln promoted the freedom of settlers within territories to determine the slave status of their new state.
(B) Lincoln passed the Homestead Act to give free land to all western settlers.
(C) Lincoln favored the exclusion of slavery from any of the new territories.
(D) Lincoln enacted the policy of giving newly freed enslaved people “forty acres and a mule.”
items.explanation: Douglass's 1857 speech charges that the entire federal government is pledged to defend slavery — yet in 1860 Lincoln ran on a platform of excluding slavery from the territories, putting federal power against slavery's expansion. Lincoln's free-soil position directly contradicted Douglass's portrait of a government wholly owned by the slave power. The Republican platform proved the federal government could be turned against slavery's spread.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Letting settlers decide was popular sovereignty, the Democratic position — not Lincoln's 1860 platform.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Homestead Act came in 1862, after the election, and was not the 1860 contradiction of Douglass.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Lincoln's 1860 platform — excluding slavery from the territories — contradicted Douglass's claim of a proslavery federal government.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Forty acres and a mule was a wartime proposal, not Lincoln's 1860 position.

items.stem: The trend in the table helped prompt which development of the era?
options: (A) the creation of federal agencies overseeing farm production and limiting output.
(B) Lower tariffs to stimulate trade and cut surpluses
(C) Farmers organizing networks to resist corporate market control
(D) Big producers building a transcontinental railroad
items.explanation: The table shows the agricultural distress of the late nineteenth century — falling crop prices and farmer indebtedness. The development it helped prompt was farmers organizing into networks to resist corporate market control: the Grange, the Farmers' Alliances, and ultimately the Populist movement. Squeezed by railroads, elevator operators, and banks, farmers built collective organizations to fight back.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Federal farm agencies limiting output came with the New Deal, not this era.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Lower tariffs were not the farmers' organized response to the conditions in the table.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The trend prompted farmers to organize networks — Grange, Alliances, Populists — resisting corporate market control.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Big producers building railroads was the problem farmers faced, not their response to it.

items.stem: The poster's imagery was designed primarily to

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1899 poster (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 49–52 refer to the following poster.

[An 1890s Buffalo Bill's Wild West show poster depicts cowboys, Native American performers, and sharpshooters on horseback circling a stagecoach, beneath the banner 'Buffalo Bill's Wild West — Congress of Rough Riders of the World.']

options: A. Document actual frontier life with strict accuracy
B. Romanticize the West for eastern and European audiences
C. Recruit soldiers to fight in the Indian Wars
D. Promote investment in railroad bonds
items.explanation: The poster's heroic cowboys, vast landscapes, and romantic frontier scenes were not documentary — they were advertising. Such imagery was designed to romanticize the West for eastern and European audiences: potential tourists, readers, and settlers who would buy the myth. The poster sold a dream of the frontier, not its reality.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The imagery was romanticized, not strictly accurate documentation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The poster's imagery was designed to romanticize the West for eastern and European audiences.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The poster was not a military recruiting tool for the Indian Wars.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. It did not promote railroad bond investment; it sold the western myth.

items.stem: The 'surplus' land provision of the Dawes Act best illustrates which of the following?

stimulus.text: "...the President of the United States [is] hereby... authorized, whenever in his opinion any reservation or any part thereof of such Indians is advantageous for agricultural and grazing purposes, to cause said reservation... to be surveyed... and to allot the lands in said reservation in severalty [separate plots of land, individually owned] to any Indian located thereon..." — Dawes Severalty Act (excerpt), 1887

options: (A) The law's primary purpose was to restore to tribes lands that had been seized through earlier fraudulent treaties.
(B) The law guaranteed that all reservation land would remain permanently under tribal ownership.
(C) The law functioned mainly as a federal jobs program for unemployed Native workers.
(D) The law's assimilationist design also served white land hunger: after allotments were made, remaining reservation land was sold to white settlers, costing tribes some 90 million acres.
items.explanation: The Dawes Act broke reservations into individual allotments, supposedly to turn Native peoples into self-sufficient farmers — assimilation through private property. But the 'surplus' provision revealed the other purpose: once allotments were assigned, the leftover reservation land was declared surplus and sold to white settlers. Between allotment and surplus sales, tribes lost some 90 million acres. Assimilation was the justification; white land hunger was the engine.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The law did not restore seized lands; it broke up the reservations tribes still held.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The law did the opposite — it dissolved tribal ownership into individual plots and sold the rest.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Dawes Act was not a jobs program; it was a land-allotment and assimilation policy.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The surplus provision shows the law's assimilationist design also served white land hunger, costing tribes some 90 million acres.

items.stem: Twain describes himself as formerly 'a red-hot imperialist.' What changed his view?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Puck, 1899-01-25 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific... But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines."
—Mark Twain, 1900 (abridged)

options: A. Reading the Treaty of Paris convinced him the U.S. meant to subjugate, not free, the Filipinos
B. He traveled to the Philippines and witnessed the war
C. He was offered a diplomatic post by the administration
D. He lost personal investments in Philippine ventures
items.explanation: Twain initially supported annexing the Philippines, but reading the Treaty of Paris changed his mind: its terms showed the United States intended to rule the Filipinos, not liberate them. The treaty transferred sovereignty from Spain to America with no provision for Filipino independence. Twain concluded the war was conquest dressed as liberation — and became America's fiercest anti-imperialist voice.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Reading the Treaty of Paris convinced Twain the U.S. meant to subjugate, not free, the Filipinos.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Twain did not travel to the Philippines; his conversion came from reading the treaty's terms.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. No diplomatic post changed Twain's view; the treaty's imperial terms did.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Twain lost no Philippine investments; his objection was moral and political.

items.stem: Consistent with the image above, Irish immigrants to the United States during the 19th century largely sought out settlement within

stimulus.text: Density of Distribution of the Natives of Ireland: 1890, Government release of 11th Census Results, 1898. [Described: a pair of statistical maps (U.S. Census Office, 1898, public domain) showing where Irish-born residents lived in 1890. The darkest shading — the heaviest concentrations of Irish natives relative to population — falls over the industrial Northeast and the Great Lakes port cities, with far lighter shading across the rural South and the far West.]

options: (A) industrialized towns and cities
(B) plantations and mostly agrarian society
(C) the American West
(D) port cities
items.explanation: The 1890 census maps show Irish-born Americans concentrated in the industrial Northeast and Great Lakes cities — the factory towns where mill and railroad jobs awaited. Fleeing famine with little money, the Irish settled where work was: industrial towns and cities, not farms or plantations. Urban industrial America was the Irish immigrant's destination.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Irish immigrants largely settled in industrialized towns and cities, where factory work was available.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Irish did not settle on plantations or in agrarian society; they were urban workers.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The far West shows light Irish settlement on the maps; the concentration was eastern and industrial.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Port cities alone are too narrow — the maps show broad industrial towns and cities, not just ports.

items.stem: The federal government subsidized the transcontinental railroad with lavish land grants because

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photograph by A. J. Russell, 1869 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the illustration described below.

The famous 1869 photograph of the Golden Spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah: two locomotives face each other, their cowcatchers nearly touching, while railroad workers, officials, and a military band crowd around the tracks where the final spike joins the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines.

options: A. It wanted to promote western settlement
B. It needed to move troops during the Civil War
C. Senators wanted to aid steel-industry backers
D. Politicians hoped to relieve unemployment
items.explanation: Congress showered the transcontinental railroads with land grants — checkerboarded millions of acres along the routes — because it wanted the West settled. Railroads would carry settlers in, carry crops and cattle out, and bind the continent together. The grants were an investment in western settlement: give the railroads land, and they would fill the West with farms and towns.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The federal government subsidized the railroads with land grants to promote western settlement.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Moving Civil War troops was not the reason; the grants aimed at peacetime settlement and development.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Aiding steel backers was not the stated purpose; western settlement was.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Relieving unemployment was not the motive; populating and developing the West was.

items.stem: The “Ghost Dance” movement among Western Native Americans stressed all of the following EXCEPT
options: (A) the belief that the world would soon come to an end
(B) the rejection of alcohol and other trappings of white society
(C) unity among Native Americans of different tribes
(D) nonviolence
items.explanation: The Ghost Dance, spreading from Wovoka's 1890 vision, preached that the world would soon end, that Native peoples should reject alcohol and white ways, and that all tribes should unite in the dance. What it did not stress was nonviolence as doctrine: the movement's apocalyptic expectation — whites swept away, ancestors returning — and the belief that ghost shirts could stop bullets gave it militant overtones that terrified white authorities. The emphasis was on the coming cataclysm and unity, not on peacefulness.

option_explanations.A: The movement did stress this, so it is not the answer. Belief in the world's imminent end was central to the Ghost Dance.
option_explanations.B: The movement did stress this, so it is not the answer. Rejecting alcohol and white trappings was core to its message.
option_explanations.C: The movement did stress this, so it is not the answer. Intertribal unity in the dance was fundamental.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The Ghost Dance did not stress nonviolence; its apocalyptic vision and bulletproof-shirt beliefs carried militant implications.

items.stem: Long's assassination in 1935

stimulus.text:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following excerpt.

Senator Huey Long charged that a tiny elite hoarded the nation's wealth while millions suffered in the Depression. He proposed capping personal fortunes, guaranteeing every family a homestead and a minimum annual income, shortening the workweek, and providing free college and old-age pensions — all funded by steep taxes on the rich.
—After Huey P. Long, 'Share Our Wealth' radio address, February 1934 (paraphrased)

options: A. Removed the leading left-populist challenger to the New Deal
B. Led to Long's election as president in 1936
C. Caused the Supreme Court to strike down the NRA as unconstitutional
D. Triggered American entry into World War II
items.explanation: Huey Long's Share Our Wealth movement made him the most dangerous challenger to Franklin Roosevelt's left — a populist demagogue promising to soak the rich and give every family a homestead and income. Roosevelt feared Long could split the Democratic vote in 1936. Long's assassination in September 1935 removed that threat, clearing Roosevelt's path to reelection.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Long's assassination removed the leading left-populist challenger to the New Deal.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Long was assassinated in 1935; he could not be elected president in 1936.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Supreme Court struck down the NRA for constitutional reasons, unrelated to Long's death.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. American entry into World War II came in 1941, years after Long's assassination.

items.stem: Which was NOT a reason for wartime hatred of the Japanese?

stimulus.pd_rationale: U.S. War Relocation Authority photograph by Dorothea Lange, 1942-05-08 (U.S. federal work); Public domain tag on Commons; NARA record 537523.

options: A. The bombing of Pearl Harbor
B. Visible physical difference
C. Outrage over the Bataan Death March from the start
D. Venomous press and film portrayals
items.explanation: Wartime hatred of the Japanese was fed by Pearl Harbor, by visible racial difference that made stereotyping easy, and by venomous press and film portrayals. Outrage over the Bataan Death March was real — but it came later: the march happened in 1942 and full details reached the American public well into the war. It was not a reason for hatred from the start.

option_explanations.A: This was a reason, so it is not the answer. Pearl Harbor ignited immediate fury.
option_explanations.B: This was a reason, so it is not the answer. Physical difference fueled racist stereotyping.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the NOT. Outrage over Bataan developed later in the war, not from the start.
option_explanations.D: This was a reason, so it is not the answer. Venomous media portrayals spread hatred.

items.stem: Garvey's message differed from that of contemporaries like W. E. B. Du Bois chiefly in its emphasis on which of the following?

stimulus.text: Marcus Garvey argued around 1924 that Black people, like all races, had souls, passions, and hopes, and that just as Canadians claimed Canada for the Canadians and Americans America for the Americans, it was reasonable for Black people worldwide to claim Africa for the Africans. — paraphrased from Marcus Garvey, speech, c. 1924

options: (A) A rejection of all political activity by Black Americans.
(B) Separate Black nationhood and racial pride rather than integration into American society.
(C) Support for Booker T. Washington's program of accommodation.
(D) A call for violent revolution within the United States.
items.explanation: Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association preached Black nationhood: Africa for the Africans, racial pride, economic self-reliance, and ultimately a separate Black state. Du Bois and the NAACP sought integration and equal rights within American society. The chief difference was separatism versus integration — Garvey wanted a nation of their own; Du Bois wanted a fair share of this one.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Garvey was intensely political — he built a mass movement, not a retreat from politics.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Garvey emphasized separate Black nationhood and racial pride rather than integration into American society.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Garvey rejected Washington's accommodationism; he demanded nationhood, not patience.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Garvey did not call for violent revolution in the United States; his program was emigration and nation-building.

items.stem: The passage's detailed account of one woman's budget exemplifies which journalistic technique?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photograph by Jacob Riis, 1888 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)

options: A. Publishing government statistics
B. Endorsing political candidates
C. Using one person's story to illustrate a widespread problem
D. Writing fictional short stories
items.explanation: The passage tells one woman's detailed budget story — her wages, her rent, her choices — to make a broad economic problem concrete and human. That is the classic muckraking technique: use one person's story to illustrate a widespread problem, letting readers feel what statistics only state. The individual case carries the general argument.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The passage uses a personal story, not government statistics.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The passage does not endorse candidates; it illustrates a social problem.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The passage uses one person's story to illustrate a widespread problem.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The story is presented as real reporting, not fiction.

items.stem: The audience for Roosevelt’s speech likely would have been most supportive of which of the following policies of the Roosevelt administration?

stimulus.text: “It is not enough to be well-meaning and kindly, but weak; neither is it enough to be strong, unless morality and decency go hand in hand with strength. We must possess the qualities which make us do our duty in our homes and among our neighbors, and in addition we must possess the qualities which are indispensable to the make-up of every great and masterful nation—the qualities of courage and hardihood, of individual initiative and yet of power to combine for a common end, and above all, the resolute determination to permit no man and no set of men to sunder us one from the other by lines of caste or creed or section. We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. There must be ever present in our minds the fundamental truth that in a republic such as ours the only safety is to stand neither for nor against any man because he is rich or because he is poor, because he is engaged in one occupation or another, because he works with his brains or because he works with his hands. We must treat each man on his worth and merits as a man. We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.” Source: Theodore Roosevelt, a speech to farmers in New York, 1903

options: (A) The creation of the National Parks system
(B) The break-up of the Northern Securities railroad trust
(C) The creation of the Food and Drug Administration
(D) The negotiation of settlements between organized labor and capital
items.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt's 1903 Square Deal speech promised fairness — a square deal for every man, neither favoring nor punishing wealth. The audience hearing that message would most support his trust-busting: the Northern Securities case (1904), in which Roosevelt broke up a giant railroad holding company. Attacking concentrated corporate power was the Square Deal's most famous application.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. National parks were a Roosevelt passion, but the speech's fairness theme points to trust-busting.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Square Deal audience would most support breaking up the Northern Securities railroad trust.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Food and Drug Administration came later (1906) and is less directly tied to this speech's theme.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Labor-capital settlements were part of Roosevelt's record, but trust-busting best matches the square-deal message.

items.stem: Notably absent from Truman's announcement is

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

President Truman's August 1945 announcement told the nation that an American plane had dropped a single bomb on Hiroshima with explosive force equal to more than 20,000 tons of TNT — a weapon, he said, that would shorten the agony of war.
—After President Harry Truman's press release, August 6, 1945

options: A. Any mention of Pearl Harbor
B. Any description of the bomb's power
C. Any reference to future bomb production
D. Any mention of the Soviet Union's entry into the war against Japan
items.explanation: Truman's August 6, 1945 announcement described the Hiroshima bomb's unprecedented power and its promise to shorten the war — but said nothing about the Soviet Union's entry into the war against Japan, which had come just as the bomb fell. The Soviet declaration of war was a major development Truman's statement notably omitted. The announcement was about the bomb, not the broader strategic picture.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Pearl Harbor was the war's origin, but the question asks what the announcement omitted — the Soviet entry.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The announcement did describe the bomb's power in detail.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Future bomb production was not the notable omission.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Notably absent was any mention of the Soviet Union's entry into the war against Japan.

items.stem: A historian could use this political cartoon to prove which of the following claims?

stimulus.text: [Described image — 1933 political cartoon titled ‘Strike-Breaking’ (original artwork not reproduced). Two burly thugs, one labeled ‘STRIKE-BREAKING’ and the other ‘UNION-BUSTING,’ beat a helpless worker with clubs. In the foreground, a small figure labeled ‘FACT-FINDING’ — a government investigator — crawls on all fours holding a magnifying glass, deliberately looking away from the violence. The cartoon charges that employers violently repressed unions while the federal government offered only a willfully blind, ineffectual ‘fact-finding’ response.]

options: (A) Supporters of organized labor were critical of government policies around unions.
(B) Companies often violently attacked workers who tried to unionize.
(C) Workers at unionized shops tended to enjoy better working conditions than those at non-unionized shops.
(D) Capitalists were unfairly maligned by radical labor unions.
items.explanation: The 1933 Strike-Breaking cartoon shows thugs labeled strike-breaking and union-busting beating a worker while a government fact-finder looks the other way. A historian could use it to prove that organized labor's supporters saw government policy as complicit — offering only willfully blind investigations while employers used violence. The cartoon is evidence of labor's critique of the state's failure to protect unions.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The cartoon proves supporters of organized labor were critical of government policies around unions — the fact-finder looks away.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The cartoon shows violence, but its argument — its provable claim — is labor's criticism of government inaction.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The cartoon says nothing about working conditions at union versus non-union shops.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The cartoon attacks capitalists; it does not show them unfairly maligned.

items.stem: America did little to check Hitler in the 1930s because
options: A. America focused on Pacific diplomacy
B. America was absorbed in domestic problems
C. The Nye Committee soured Americans on intervention
D. Both B and C
items.explanation: In the 1930s, America was absorbed in the Depression — a quarter of the workforce unemployed — and the Nye Committee's investigations had convinced many that arms makers had dragged the country into World War I. Domestic crisis plus disillusionment with intervention produced isolationism. Both factors together explain why America did little to check Hitler: it was consumed at home and soured on foreign crusades.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Pacific diplomacy was not the reason for inaction against Hitler; domestic absorption and anti-interventionism were.
option_explanations.B: True, but only part of the answer. Domestic problems absorbed America, and the Nye Committee soured it on intervention.
option_explanations.C: True, but only part of the answer. The Nye Committee's findings fed isolationism alongside domestic crisis.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Both B and C explain American inaction: domestic problems and Nye Committee-fueled anti-interventionism.

items.stem: The Yippies' use of media spectacle most directly anticipated

stimulus.text:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

Abbie Hoffman recalled storming the Pentagon in 1967 — leaping fences with fellow protesters in a theatrical, chaotic demonstration meant to dramatize opposition to the Vietnam War.
—After Abbie Hoffman, on the 1967 Pentagon march

options: A. The decline of television news
B. Later protest movements' use of viral media stunts
C. Government censorship of newspapers
D. The end of nominating conventions
items.explanation: The Yippies — Abbie Hoffman, Jerry Rubin — staged theatrical protests designed for television cameras: the Pentagon levitation attempt, pie-throwing, guerrilla theater. They understood that spectacle earned airtime, and airtime spread the message. That logic directly anticipated later protest movements' use of viral media stunts — demonstrations choreographed for cameras and shares rather than for the officials in the room.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Television news did not decline; the Yippies exploited its growth.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Yippies' media spectacles anticipated later movements' viral media stunts.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Government censorship of newspapers was not what the Yippies' tactics foreshadowed.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Nominating conventions continued; the Yippies' legacy was in protest media, not convention procedure.

items.stem: The Army-McCarthy hearings proved

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-Congress}}: work of the U.S. Congress. Public domain.

options: A. Americans cared little about communism
B. Eisenhower would back McCarthy unconditionally
C. McCarthy had little proof for his charges
D. McCarthy's massive popularity
items.explanation: The 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings, televised to millions, exposed Joseph McCarthy bullying witnesses and produced Joseph Welch's famous have you no decency rebuke. The hearings proved McCarthy had little proof for his charges — his lists and numbers collapsed under scrutiny. Public support evaporated, and the Senate soon censured him.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Americans cared deeply about communism; the hearings discredited McCarthy, not the concern.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Eisenhower privately opposed McCarthy and did not back him unconditionally.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The hearings proved McCarthy had little proof for his charges.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The hearings destroyed, not demonstrated, McCarthy's popularity.

items.stem: Eisenhower's presidency most resembled that of
options: A. Franklin Roosevelt
B. William Howard Taft
C. Calvin Coolidge
D. Theodore Roosevelt
items.explanation: Dwight Eisenhower's presidency — cautious, business-friendly, fiscally conservative, devoted to limited government — most resembled Calvin Coolidge's. Both were restrained conservatives who believed government's business was to stay out of business's way. Eisenhower was no activist like the Roosevelts; he was a consolidator in the Coolidge mold.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Franklin Roosevelt was the great activist; Eisenhower was his temperamental opposite.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Taft was a trust-busting progressive Republican, not Eisenhower's model.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Eisenhower's restrained, business-friendly conservatism most resembled Calvin Coolidge's.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Theodore Roosevelt was a crusading activist; Eisenhower governed quietly.

items.stem: All of the following threatened Harry Truman’s chances for re-election in 1948 EXCEPT

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-US-not-renewed}}: U.S. work whose copyright was not renewed. Public domain.

options: (A) Truman’s positions on civil rights
(B) rampant inflation
(C) the Dixiecrat candidacy of Strom Thurmond
(D) public dissatisfaction with the Korean War
items.explanation: Truman's 1948 reelection was threatened by his civil rights program (which drove Southern Democrats to bolt), by rampant postwar inflation, and by Strom Thurmond's Dixiecrat candidacy splitting the South. Public dissatisfaction with the Korean War was not among these threats — the war began in 1950, two years after the election. Korea could not have endangered a 1948 campaign.

option_explanations.A: This did threaten Truman, so it is not the answer. Civil rights drove the Dixiecrat bolt.
option_explanations.B: This did threaten Truman, so it is not the answer. Inflation hurt his standing.
option_explanations.C: This did threaten Truman, so it is not the answer. Thurmond's candidacy split the Democratic South.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The Korean War began in 1950, after the 1948 election.

items.stem: According to her testimony, Bentley's Soviet contacts had obtained

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

Questioner: Can you describe the military information you obtained through the Silvermaster group? Bentley: I passed along classified material on aircraft production and other defense matters, gathered from government employees sympathetic to the Soviet cause.
—After Elizabeth Bentley's testimony before the House Committee on Un-American Activities, 1948

options: A. Detailed inside information on U.S. aircraft production and military plans, including D-Day
B. The design secrets of the atomic bomb
C. The identities of HUAC's own members
D. Advance plans for the Marshall Plan
items.explanation: Elizabeth Bentley — the confessed Soviet courier who testified before HUAC in 1948 — described passing along classified material on aircraft production and defense matters gathered from government employees. Her testimony claimed Soviet contacts had obtained detailed inside information on U.S. aircraft production and military plans, including D-Day preparations. It was the insider-espionage story that fueled the era's spy panic.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Bentley testified her Soviet contacts obtained detailed inside information on aircraft production and military plans, including D-Day.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Atomic bomb secrets were the Rosenberg case, not Bentley's testimony.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Bentley did not reveal the identities of HUAC's own members.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Marshall Plan advance plans were not what Bentley described passing.

items.stem: The passage provides the classic rationale for which U.S. Cold War strategy?
